Liwanag

A GED108 Art Appreciation Portfolio

Liwanag means light. From a night sky by Van Gogh to a desk lit by a laptop, this is how I learned to look, explore, and create.

By Karlo Angelo Babaran, Mapúa uOX, 2026

Stage 1: Look

Lessons 1 to 3. Learning the language of art: elements, principles, and how to read a painting.

Visual Analysis

Two ways of reading art: a full analysis of one painting, and three short studies of the elements and principles of design.

Exam 1

The Starry Night (1889), Vincent van Gogh

I laid out the analysis as an infographic: description, the artist, the elements of art (color, line, shape, texture, space), the principles of design (contrast, emphasis, unity, movement, balance), then interpretation and evaluation. My central message: even in the darkest night, there is still light, movement, and hope.

Click the image to read it in full.

Conceptualize, Assignment 1

Stage 2: Explore

Lessons 5 to 8. Moving through art history and into the Van Gogh Museum.

Virtual Museum Visit: Van Gogh Museum

  • Museum: Van Gogh Museum
  • Location: Amsterdam, Netherlands
  • Activities: scavenger hunt, meme, sketch, reflection
Sketch

The Bedroom (1888)

My colored-pencil study of the artwork that spoke to me most. The museum explains that Van Gogh used bright colors here to express rest and comfort, and drawing it made me notice the tilted perspective and the visible lines of the floorboards.

Scavenger hunt

I found an artwork for 15 categories, from the most vibrant (Sunflowers) and the strangest (Skull of a Skeleton with Burning Cigarette) to the one I would like to step into (The Bedroom).

Make a meme

"Me pretending everything is fine after saying 'I'll only study for 10 minutes.'" Skull of a Skeleton with Burning Cigarette, Van Gogh, 1886.

Reflection

Impression

Bright and exciting, with visible brushstrokes and a clear view of how his style changed over time.

Favorite

The Bedroom: simple on the surface, full of color, and relaxing because it shows an ordinary room.

Discovery

Van Gogh used color, line, and brushwork to show his own emotions and the feelings of the people he painted.

Stage 3: Create

Lessons 9 and 10. Turning what I learned into art of my own.

Photo Essay: My Mapúa uOX Journey

A scrapbook-style collage of my daily life as an online student.

Four photos follow one routine: opening my tablet, working through lessons on the laptop, taking notes taped near my desk, and finishing tasks with earphones on. Red arrows guide the eye from one photo to the next, so the collage reads like a story.

I used torn paper, tape, and doodles (a light bulb, a laptop, a graduation cap) to give the layout energy, and the red, black, and gold palette to match the school's identity. The sketches of campus buildings in the corners remind the viewer that online learning still belongs to a real place.

Learning happens anywhere, even in the corner of my room.

More Creative Work

Photo Appropriation

The Starry Sketch (2026)

I reimagined Van Gogh's The Starry Night as a digital sketch that shows an artist walking through the swirling sky.

Kind

Motif and style appropriation: I borrowed the swirling sky, stars, and hills, then retold them in a narrative sketch.

Issue

How modern artists draw on historical icons and on a heritage of struggle, introspection, and creative vision.

Message

Art appreciation is a dialogue, not passive viewing. Creators can find strength in legacy and express their inner worlds through reimagined classics.

Art Talk

My Art: Video Gaming

A talk on gaming as my own art form, illustrated with two sketches inspired by Van Gogh. A game, like a room or a sky in a painting, is a designed world where every color and object is chosen on purpose.

Presentation

Surrealism: Revolutionizing Reality Through the Unconscious

Surrealism grew out of Dada in 1920s Paris and was codified by André Breton's 1924 Manifesto. It responded to the horror of World War I, drew on Freud's ideas about dreams and desire, and opposed colonialism. I studied its key figures and methods.

  • André Breton
  • Meret Oppenheim
  • Max Ernst
  • Salvador Dalí
  • Psychic automatism
  • Chance and found objects
  • Film and photography

Lessons Learned from GED108

What changed in the way I see art, and the world around it.

The humanities matter

Lesson 1 showed me that art and technology complement each other, and that art is part of what makes us human.

Looking is a skill

Describing before judging, as in my visual analysis, made me notice details I used to skip. The virtual museum scavenger hunt trained the same habit.

Color carries emotion

Van Gogh's clashing reds and greens in The Night Café feel uneasy, while the colors of The Bedroom feel restful. Color is a feeling before it is a hue.

Elements and principles give me words

Balance, rhythm, contrast, and emphasis let me explain why The Great Wave and Broadway Boogie Woogie work, not only that I like them.

Art is personal expression

The photo essay and Art Talk showed me that my own routine, school life, and gaming can be material for art.

Borrowing is a conversation

Appropriation taught me to respond to a classic with my own idea and credit the source, as I did with The Starry Sketch.

Art moves with its times

From ancient art to Surrealism (Lessons 5 to 8), I learned that each style answers the events and ideas of its moment, from war to psychology.

Museums are open to everyone

Visiting the Van Gogh Museum from home opened my eyes to the creativity of Van Gogh and other painters, and made art feel within reach.

Everyone is a soul maker

Lesson 10 showed me that making art is a way to shape who I am, which is what my photo essay, sketches, and gaming talk did for me.

Hope in the dark

The Starry Night reminded me that beauty can be found even during dark times, a message I carry beyond this course.

My GED108 experience taught me to find light in ordinary places.
